rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: People of the Heights seek intercession, pass from Adam through the prophets to Muhammad, enter Paradise after his intercession, bathe in the River of Life, and become the Poor of Paradise; Salim wishes he were one of them.
rows.anchor: وعن حذيفة أن أهل الأعراف يرغبون في الشفاعة فيأتون آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two groups hearing each other across the vertical distance is rationally possible, with or without sight; God may expose them to one another or place a barrier between them.
rows.anchor: وهذا يقتضي سماع كل من الفريقين كلام الآخر وهذا جائز عقلا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: After the Heights enter Paradise, Hell's people ask to see and speak with their relatives; the relatives fail to recognize their blackened, transformed kin until called by name, and refuse their plea for water or food.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنه لما صار أصحاب الأعراف إلى الجنة طمع أهل النار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The call reflects hope that the request will be granted; al-Qadi instead says it occurs despite knowledge of endless punishment, as a drowning person grasps at foam.
rows.anchor: وكلام ابن عباس يدل على أن هذا النداء كان عن رجاء وطمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Pour out” is stronger than “give us a drink,” suggesting abundant water; they are parched and burning, while food or other provision is sought because human bodies need nourishment or in hope of mercy.
rows.anchor: وأفيضوا أمكن من اسقونا لأنها تقتضي التوسعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes “or” in its ordinary alternative sense; “what God provided” can include foods, fruit, and drinks other than water. Suddī restricts it to fruit, while al-Zamakhshari means other drinks; the wording says God forbade each item.
rows.anchor: والعطف بأو يدل على أن الأول لا يندرج في العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators take “or” as “and,” in light of the response that God forbade both requests.
rows.anchor: أو بمعنى الواو لقولهم إن الله حرمهما

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He allows “what God provided” to mean food and fruit, with an implicit “throw to us”; the cited verse of poetry coordinates fodder and water under one verb.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يراد وألقوا علينا مما رزقكم الله من الطعام والفاكهة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The damned make the request in bewilderment and desperation despite expecting no answer, like a distressed person under trial.
rows.anchor: وإنما يطلبون ذلك مع يأسهم من الإجابة إليه حيرة في أمرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “forbidden” means withheld or barred, and the inhabitants report God's ruling to one another.
rows.anchor: ومعنى التحريم هنا المنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of those who made religion amusement and play has already been interpreted similarly in al-Anʿam.
rows.anchor: تقدم تفسير مثل هذا في الأنعام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: God leaves them in punishment as they neglected consideration of meeting this Day; Qatadah says they forgot good, not evil; al-Zamakhshari likens God to a master who forgets servants when withholding good.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وجماعة يتركهم في العذاب كما تركوا النظر

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and most exegetes say God leaves them in torment as they left works for the meeting with Him; the author reads the two “what” clauses as verbal nouns and “as” causally.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن والسدي أيضا والأكثرون تتركهم في عذابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to the previously mentioned disbelievers, making “Book” a generic divine scripture, or—according to Yahya ibn Sallam—to Muhammad's deniers at a new discourse, with the Book being the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وقال يحيى بن سلام الضمير لمكذبي محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We detailed it with knowledge” is explained as detailing laws, exhortations, stories, and meanings; clarifying truth from falsehood; or revealing it in distinct sections.
rows.anchor: فصلناه بإيضاح الحق من الباطل

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read “we favored it” with ḍād, meaning the Qur'an was distinguished above other books; al-Tahrir attributes thirty unique virtues to it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن والجحدري فضلناه بالضاد المنقوطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “With knowledge” is apparently circumstantial of the subject of detailing, possibly of its object if construed “containing knowledge”; “guidance and mercy” can be circumstantial, causal objects, nominative predicates, or—under Zayd ibn Ali—genitive appositives/adjectives.
rows.anchor: فصلناه صفة لكتاب وعلى علم الظاهر أنه حال من فاعل فصلناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The six days include the earth with its soil, mountains, trees, resources, light, animals, and Adam, matching the sound hadith; they remain six ordinary days distinguished by sunrise and sunset.
rows.anchor: فيكون في ستة أيام مدة لخلق الأرض بتربتها وجبالها

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some interpret God's settling on the Throne literally as His self's establishment there; most early authorities instead affirm the transmitted attributes without specifying God's intended meaning, while another group offers figurative interpretations.
rows.anchor: من الاستقرار بذاته على العرش قوم والجمهور من السلف

rows.speaker: سفيان الثوري
rows.claim: Sufyan al-Thawri interprets “settled” as God performing an act on the Throne that He calls settling.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان الثوري فعل فعلا في العرش سماه استواء

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل بن النحوي
rows.claim: He derives “Throne” as a verbal noun from “to erect”; the author's ensuing note says this does not fit the scriptural understanding of the Throne as a particular created body.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي الفضل بن النحوي أنه قال العرش مصدر عرش يعرش عرشا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Throne” has several lexical senses: royal seat, roof or anything elevated and sheltering, sovereignty, a well's wooden frame, four stars below al-ʿAwwāʾ, and the upper foot by the toes; poetry attests the sovereignty sense.
rows.anchor: فالعرش سرير الملك ومنه ورفع أبويه على العرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Settled” can mean settled, risen, intended, equaled, or become equal; “prevailed” is also proposed, but Ibn al-Aʿrabi says he knows no use of “settled” meaning “prevailed,” despite the cited poetic evidence.
rows.anchor: واستوى أيضا يستعمل بمعنى استقر وبمعنى علا وبمعنى قصد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject pronoun in “then settled upon the Throne” need not be God: it may refer to creation understood from “created,” including in “the All-Merciful settled,” so the verse does not compel a literal reading.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله ثم استوى على العرش يحتمل أن يعود على المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given the ambiguity of “Throne,” “settled,” and its pronoun, and rational arguments against bodily establishment, the verse need not be read literally; al-Hasan says God's command prevailed.
rows.anchor: ومع الاحتمال في العرش وفي استوى وفي الضمير العائد لا يتعين حمل الآية

rows.speaker: مالك بن أنس
rows.claim: When asked how God settled, Malik said the settling is known, its modality inconceivable, belief in it obligatory, and questioning it an innovation; he had the asker expelled as misguided.
rows.anchor: الاستواء معلوم والكيف غير معقول والإيمان به واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He covers the night with the day” means night removes daylight so earthly life can function, with night for rest and day for activity; the causative verb takes two objects.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أنه يذهب الليل نور النهار ليتم قوام الحياة في الدنيا

rows.speaker: الأخوان
rows.claim: The Two (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Abu Bakr read the verb with gemination; the remaining Seven read it with a still ghayn. Hamid ibn Qays has a further reading reported differently by al-Dani and Ibn Jinni.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بالتضعيف الأخوان وأبو بكر وبإسكان الغين باقي السبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against Ibn ʿAtiyya's preference for Ibn Jinni's report, the author favors al-Dani's reading report as more apt: night is the semantic agent even when grammatically made an object by causation.
rows.anchor: والذي نقله أبو عمرو الداني عن حميد أمكن من حيث المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Pursuing it swiftly” may describe night as the circumstantial semantic agent, day as the pursued patient, or an omitted verbal noun; pursuit is metaphor for the uninterrupted alternation, and night is mentioned first as elsewhere.
rows.anchor: ونسبة الطلب إلى الليل مجازية وهو عبارة عن تعاقبه اللازم

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says night and day alternate through the fastest, strongest motion of the outermost sphere; a runner would travel thousands of miles in that sphere's time to lift and place a foot, and the Qur'an's swimming image suggests speed, ease, and continuity.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي وصف هذه الحركة بالسرعة والشدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Subdued by His command” is circumstantial of sun, moon, and stars; Ibn ʿAmir raises all four words, while Aban ibn Thaʿlab raises only “stars” and “subdued.” God's command means His will and governance, likened to orders.
rows.anchor: ومعنى بأمره بمشيئته وتصريفه وهو متعلق بمسخرات

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi distinguishes the sun's own annual movement, which makes the year, from its daily movement with the outermost sphere; therefore night and day arise from the heaven's motion, not the sun's.
rows.anchor: الشمس لها نوعان من الحركة أحدهما بحسب ذاتها وذلك يتم في سنة كاملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi infers that the Throne/outermost sphere drives the other spheres and planets contrary to their natures, while the sun's overpowering force makes it able to move them; the author calls these rational inquiries suggested by the Qur'an and ends with “God knows best.”
rows.anchor: فهذه أبحاث معقولة ولفظ القرآن مشعر بها والعلم عند الله

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab relates the word “zحف” to the poetic meter defect in which a letter is dropped and the next shifts toward it.
rows.anchor: وقال ثعلب ومنه الزحاف في الشعر وهو أن يسقط من الحرفين

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth defines a “zحف” as a mass moving toward its enemy; al-Aʿsha's verse compares it to a ship pushing forward.
rows.anchor: الجماعة يمشون إلى عدوهم هو الزحف

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ defines “zحف” as a slow approach and gives forms for moving toward battle; a Hidhli poem likens snake tracks to whip marks.
rows.anchor: الزحف الدنو قليلا يقال زحف إليه يزحف زحفا إذا مشى

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: “Mutahayyiz” means joined to a side; Abu ʿUbayda equates “tahayyuz” and “tahawwuz” with withdrawing.
rows.anchor: التحيز والتحوز التنحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Throwing is done with an arrow, stone, or dirt; “makāʾ” means whistling, illustrated by the cited verse and animal sound, while al-Suddi identifies it as a white bird in the Hijaz.
rows.anchor: مكت است الدابة إذا نفخت بالريح

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda and others define “maka” as whistling; the author notes that sound nouns commonly follow the pattern faʿāl, such as shouting, roaring, and barking.
rows.anchor: مكا يمكو مكاء إذا صفر والكثير في الأصوات أن تكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Tasdiyah” means clapping and derives from the sound ṣadā; “rakm” is piling things up, and “maḍā” means passed or advanced, with maḍī as its verbal noun.
rows.anchor: التصدية التصفيق صدى يصدي تصدية صفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to stand firm follows God's report that He casts fear into the enemy and the command to strike them; “zحفًا” may describe the enemy's multitude, the Muslims as an advancing army, or the opposing lines approaching each other.
rows.anchor: مناسبة هذه الآية لما قبلها أنه تعالى لما أخبر أنه سيلقي الرعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis takes “zحفًا” as an implicit verbal noun; another says the command was initially to withstand ten enemies, then was eased to one Muslim for two, while the first calls the prohibition firm and absolute.
rows.anchor: وقيل انتصب زحفا على المصدر بحال محذوفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Backs” is chosen instead of a neutral word for turning to make flight ugly and shameful; the prohibition also commands steadfastness and endurance.
rows.anchor: وعدل عن الظهور إلى لفظ الأدبار تقبيحا لفعل الفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poem depicts fighters' wounds on their feet rather than their heels, illustrating that they did not turn their backs in flight.
rows.anchor: فلسنا على الأعقاب تجري كلومنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tahrir calls the indirect disparagement “taʿrīḍ,” “imāʾ,” or “kināyah”; the author rejects “kināyah” here because that device states a beautiful expression for an ugly meaning.
rows.anchor: وهذا النوع من علم البيان يسمى بالتعريض عرض بسوء حالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some restrict “that day” to Badr and say the weakness verse later abrogated the rule; the author objects that Badr is covered by the conditional if the verse came before its end, but cannot be covered if revelation came afterward.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول بأن الإشارة بقوله يومئذ إلى يوم بدر لا يظهر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya and the majority take the referent as any day the encounter mentioned in the condition occurs; the rule remains, calibrated by the later limit of one Muslim facing two, and was not abrogated.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية والجمهور على أنه إشارة إلى يوم اللقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that Uhud's retreat was from positions under pressure while the Prophet remained among them, and Hunayn involved breaking ranks before turning back; he allows that God's pardon for Uhud may concern their multitude.
rows.anchor: وأما يوم أحد فإنما فر الناس من مراكزهم من ضعفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads “rear” with a still bāʾ; “turning to fight” and “joining a force” are circumstantial accusatives of the pronoun in “whoever turns.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن دبره بسكون الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls “except” redundant or an exception from turners; Ibn ʿAtiyya says it is from the turners. The author says it instead excludes from an omitted general state, since exception needs an implicit general term in this positive conditional.
rows.anchor: والتقدير: ومن يولهم ملتبسا بأية حالة إلا في حال

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A combat feint is turning away as if retreating, then wheeling back on the enemy; it is a stratagem for someone who judges it more damaging and advantageous.
rows.anchor: والتحرف للقتال هو الكر بعد الفر يخيل عدوه أنه منهزم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The “faction” is generally a body of people at war; joining another Muslim unit can reinforce a weaker line, while the discussion also allows a target enemy group when the retreat improves the fighter's impact.
rows.anchor: والفئة هنا قال الجمهور هي الجماعة من الناس الحاضرة للحرب

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Some explain the faction as the city, imam, or Muslim community wherever it is; when a Qadisiyya deserter reached Madinah, ʿUmar told him, “I am your faction.”
rows.anchor: انهزم رجل من القادسية فأتى المدينة إلى عمر رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar and other raiders fled, then asked the Prophet if they were deserters; he called them returners and said, “I am your faction.” Thaʿlab glosses “returners” as those who wheel back.
rows.anchor: خرجت سرية وأنا فيهم ففروا فلما رجعوا إلى المدينة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls flight from battle one of the gravest major sins; Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet listing it among the seven destructive sins.
rows.anchor: الفرار من الزحف من أكبر الكبائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tahrir limits the threatened flight to desertion while able to hold firm; withdrawal when one cannot withstand is not flight. Al-Qadi argues the warning includes sinful believers, but the author says the general text may be qualified.
rows.anchor: وفي التحرير التولي الذي وقع عليه الوعيد هو الفرار مع المصابرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text apparently permits joining a faction whether or not one's own army is large, though another view disallows it when the army is large; flight without an excuse is a major sin, and Ibn al-Qasim rejects a deserter's testimony.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه يجوز التحيز سواء عظم العسكر أم لا

rows.speaker: الحارث بن هشام
rows.claim: Al-Harith ibn Hisham defends retreat by saying that fighting alone would have killed him without harming the enemy; a verse attributed about him likewise says he escaped on a swift horse.
rows.anchor: وعلمت أني إن أقاتل واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Companions returned from Badr boasting of whom they had killed and captured, and the verse was revealed; al-Zamakhshari treats its opening as an answer to their implied boast.
rows.anchor: لما رجع الصحابة من بدر ذكروا مفاخرهم فيقول القائل قتلت وأسرت فنزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against al-Zamakhshari, the initial particle links clauses: the believers carried out the command to strike, yet did not independently create the killing; God is its creator, refuting those who assign human acts to humans as creators.
rows.anchor: وليست الفاء جواب شرط محذوف كما زعم وإنما هي للربط بين الجمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “But God killed them” balances the denial of the believers' independent killing with affirmation of God's true act; another theological reading construes their role merely as a cause while God sent angels and enabled victory.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك رد على من زعم أن أفعال العباد خلق لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired negation and affirmation are rhetorically emphatic: past denial uses “did not” with the imperfect, matching the affirmative wording and denying what was explicitly asserted; this emphasis suits the miraculous throw.
rows.anchor: وفي الجملة مبالغة من وجهين أحدهما أن النفي جاء على حسب الإيجاب لفظا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet took a handful of dirt at Badr and said “May the faces be disfigured”; every polytheist received some in eyes, mouth, and nostrils.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس قبض رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يوم بدر قبضة من تراب

rows.speaker: حكيم بن حزام
rows.claim: Hakim ibn Hizam heard a heavenly sound like a pebble dropping into a vessel; the Prophet's throw then routed the enemy. Anas instead reports three pebbles aimed at right, left, and center.
rows.anchor: وقال حكيم بن حزام فسمعنا صوتا من السماء كأنه صوت حصاة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: A report identifies the throw as the Prophet's spear against Ubayy ibn Khalaf at Uhud; Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects it as weak because the verse followed Badr, so the Uhud explanation would be contextually disconnected.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف لأن الآية نزلت عقب بدر وعلى هذا القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To reconcile “you did not throw” with “when you threw,” interpreters distinguish the denied outcome (hitting, victory, or taking life) from the affirmed sending or wounding; another says the Prophet did not act independently in sending the dirt.
rows.anchor: فالمنفي الإصابة والظفر والمثبت الإرسال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says the Prophet's arrow at Khaybar hit Ibn Abi al-Huqayq; the author rejects it as false and says the correct account of that man's killing differs.
rows.anchor: وهذا فاسد والصحيح في صورة قتل ابن أبي الحقيق غير هذا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi interprets the good trial as God supporting and favoring the believers; “bala” can mean good or hardship, but “good” here points to victory and honor. Al-Zamakhshari likewise calls it a fine gift.
rows.anchor: قال السدي ينصرهم وينعم عليهم يقال أبلاه إذا أنعم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpretations of the good trial include victory and spoils, or martyrdom for the fourteen killed at Badr. A proposed future-jihad ordeal is rejected by context, which presents God's killing and throwing as the means of victory and plunder.
rows.anchor: وقيل بالشهادة لمن استشهد يوم بدر وهم أربعة عشر رجلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God is Hearing, Knowing” answers the Companions' boasts about kills and captives: He hears their words and knows their intentions, including whether anyone fought from zeal or self-defense instead of for God's cause.
rows.anchor: فقيل إن الله سميع عليم لكلامكم وما تفخرون به عليم بما انطوت عليه الضمائر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes “that” as the favorable trial and coordinates God's weakening of the disbelievers' plan with the purpose of favoring believers; Ibn ʿAtiyya instead refers it to the preceding killing and throwing.
rows.anchor: ذلكم إشارة إلى البلاء الحسن ومحله الرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative may be nominative as “that is the matter,” or accusative for “we did that”; “that God weakens” may coordinate with the purpose or the demonstrative, or depend on an understood “know.” Al-Hufi offers further subject-predicate parses.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية ذلكم إشارة إلى ما تقدم من قتل الله ورميه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Two Medinese readers and Abu ʿAmr read “weakener” from wahana with gemination, while the others, al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʾ, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Muhaysin read it from awhana; Hafs uses annexation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان وأبو عمرو موهن من وهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If addressed to believers, “if you seek victory” promises aid, urges them to desist from their earlier handling of spoils and captives, warns that repeating it brings renewed reproach, and reassures them that numbers cannot replace God's help.
rows.anchor: فحمله قوم على أنه خطاب للمؤمنين ويؤيده قوله فقد جاءكم الفتح

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Most commentators address the Meccans sarcastically: before Badr they prayed at the Kaaba for the better of two hosts to win; reports give variant invocations, including Abu Jahl's prayer that God destroy whichever side severed kin ties.
rows.anchor: وقال الأكثرون هي خطاب لأهل مكة على سبيل التهكم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Hasan, Mujahid, and others say Quraysh made the plea while setting out to protect the caravan; al-Nadr ibn al-Harith also called the Qur'an's claim true if it was revelation, and was killed at Badr.
rows.anchor: كان هذا القول من قريش وقت خروجهم لنصرة العير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Meccan reading, the promised victory came to Muslims over them; alternatively it means the decisive judgment that made the truth clear. Desisting means ending disbelief, and renewed combat brings Muslim victory and their defeat.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا القول يكون معنى قوله فقد جاءكم الفتح ولكنه كان للمسلمين عليكم

rows.speaker: الفرقة
rows.claim: Another group takes the first clause as addressed to Muslims and “if you desist” to disbelievers: ending hostility is better for them, but renewed war brings God's support to the Messenger.
rows.anchor: إن تستفتحوا خطاب للمؤمنين وإن تنتهوا خطاب للكافرين

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani narrows desisting to ending the dispute over Badr's spoils and ransom for captives; renewed disobedience brings renewed divine censure. A variant reads “will not avail” in masculine, with separation licensing it.
rows.anchor: وإن تنتهوا عن أمر الأنفال وفداء الأسرى ببدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ensuing address urges sincere believers, honoring them, to obey God and the Messenger in jihad or all commands; reading it as aimed at hypocrites or Israelites is rejected as either inconsistent with faith or contextually unrelated.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه نداء وخطاب للمؤمنين الخلص حثهم بالأمر على طاعة الله ورسوله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The pronoun in “do not turn away from him” may refer to the Messenger, the command to obey, obedience itself, or God; the author prefers the Messenger because turning away applies literally to him, while other referents are figurative.
rows.anchor: وإنما عاد على الرسول لأن التولي إنما يصح في حق الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “While you hear” is a circumstantial clause: hearing is incompatible with turning away; it may mean hearing God's admonition, commands and prohibitions, understanding, or believing.
rows.anchor: وأنتم تسمعون جملة حالية أي لا يناسب سماعكم التولي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who claimed to hear but did not may be Jews, hypocrites, polytheists, those who said they could imitate the Qur'an, Banu ʿAbd al-Dar except two converts, or al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his followers.
rows.anchor: والمشبه بهم اليهود أو المنافقون أو المشركون أو الذين قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their hearing is denied because it produced no faith; imperfect negation with “la” suggests continued refusal, whereas a past-tense denial would not convey persistence. The claims of believers make disobedience especially inconsistent.
rows.anchor: ولما لم يجد سماعهم ولا أثر فيهم نفى عنهم السماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deaf and mute are the worst creatures: deaf to the Qur'an, mute about saving faith, and lacking reason; deafness naturally produces muteness because speech is learned by hearing, as in the parallel “deaf, mute, blind.” These images signify rejection.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الصم عن ما يلقي إليهم من القرآن البكم عن الإقرار بالإيمان

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: The description appears general; alternatively it concerns Banu ʿAbd al-Dar, who claimed deafness, muteness, and blindness to Muhammad's message and died at Badr carrying the standard. Ibn Jurayj says hypocrites; al-Hasan says People of the Book.
rows.anchor: نزلت في طائفة من بني عبد الدار كانوا يقولون

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says their lack of hearing and guidance follows God's knowledge of them; “make them hear” means an understanding, guiding hearing, and if they understood, they would still turn away by prior decree.
rows.anchor: أخبر تعالى بأن عدم سماعهم وهداهم إنما هو بما علمه الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari interprets good as benefiting from divine grace; God withholds grace because it would not help them, and even if they believed through it they would later apostatize and deny.
rows.anchor: ولو علم الله في هؤلاء الصم البكم خيرا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says “He would have made them hear” means God would answer whatever they asked.
rows.anchor: لأسمعهم جواب كلما سألوا

rows.speaker: ابن الجوزي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jawzi says they asked God to make them hear the dead whom they had asked Him to bring back to life, such as Qusayy ibn Kilab, to testify to Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: لأسمعهم كلام الموتى الذين طلبوا إحياءهم

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi explains the hypothetical as: if they had good, God would let them hear proofs and exhortations in an instructive way that brings understanding.
rows.anchor: التعبير عن عدمه في نفسه بعدم علم الله بوجوده

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi adds that if God made them hear despite knowing they lacked good, they would not benefit and would turn away.
rows.anchor: ولو أسمعهم إذ علم أنه لا خير فيهم لم ينتفعوا بها

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi compares this counterfactual knowledge with Qur'anic hypotheticals about hypocrites not leaving with the believers, their failure to support them, and returned disbelievers repeating forbidden conduct.
rows.anchor: حكاية عن المنافقين لئن أخرجتم لنخرجن معكم

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi distinguishes actual knowledge from knowledge of hypothetical possibilities and puts “if He knew good in them” among counterfactuals, like the Qur'anic claims that hypocrites would not go out and that returned disbelievers would repeat their forbidden conduct.
rows.anchor: معلومات الله على أربعة أقسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two hypotheticals cannot simply be linked: if God knew good and made them hear, the text says they would turn away, yielding the contradiction that people with good would turn away. The clauses require interpretation rather than this inference.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يكون لأنه لا يقع التولي على تقدير علمه فيهم خيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet reproaches Ubay for not answering when he called him while Ubay was praying, citing the revealed command to respond to God and the Messenger.
rows.anchor: لأبي حين دعاه وهو في الصلاة متلبث

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and most commentators identify life-giving response with obeying the Qur'an's commands and prohibitions, yielding eternal life and bliss; the author prefers this in context as beneficial instruction that leads to good in both lives.
rows.anchor: المعنى استجيبوا للطاعة وما تضمنه القرآن من أوامر ونواهي

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Alternative explanations of “what gives you life” are fighting unbelievers, which prevents defeat and death; martyrdom, according to Ibn Ishaq; religious knowledge; truth, also reported from Mujahid; worldly elevation; war spoils and livelihood; or bodily life.
rows.anchor: لما يحييكم هو مجاهدة الكفار لأنهم لو تركوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial lam may attach to the Messenger's call, since “call” takes lam; others make lam mean “to” and attach it to “respond,” distinguishing the two prepositions' functions. Poetry illustrates the syntax.
rows.anchor: والظاهر تعلق لما بقوله دعاكم ودعا يتعدى باللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies ʿAli ibn ʿIsa as al-Rummani and describes his preceding interpretation as following a Muʿtazili approach.
rows.anchor: وعلي بن عيسى هو الرماني وهو معتزلي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says God may control a person's heart, turn cowardice to courage, or protect a believer from intended sins; he interprets the hadith of the heart between God's fingers as two effects of lordship. It may also mean God knows every thought.
rows.anchor: وتأويله بين أثرين من آثار ربوبيته

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari prefers that God owns hearts more completely than people do and can intervene between each person and heart by His will; the author's broader sense is God's control over all things and ability to thwart desire.
rows.anchor: واختار الطبري أن يكون المعنى إن الله أخبر أنه أملك لقلوب العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says God protects believers from sins that their hearts intend through divine preservation.
rows.anchor: يحول بين المؤمن وبين المعاصي التي يهم بها قلبه بالعصمة

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Ishaq reads “between the person” with kasra on mīm, following the inflection; Hasan and al-Zuhri read “between the person” without hamza, with the hamza's vowel shifted and r geminated by extending pause pronunciation into connected speech.
rows.anchor: بين المرء بكسر الميم إتباعا لحركة الإعراب إذ في المرء لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “and to Him you will be gathered” apparently refers to God, though it may be a pronoun of circumstance; resurrection brings reward and punishment and reminds hearers of their final outcome.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الضمير في أنه عائد إلى الله ويحتمل أن يكون ضمير الشأن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The command to fear a trial that may strike wrongdoers and others is general: Ibn ʿAbbas says believers must not tolerate wrongdoing lest punishment engulf them; Bukhari and Tirmidhi report that failure to restrain a wrongdoer risks a general divine punishment.
rows.anchor: أمر المؤمنين أن لا يقروا المنكر بين أظهرهم

rows.speaker: زينب بنت جحش
rows.claim: In Muslim, Zaynab bint Jahsh asks whether people will perish while righteous people remain among them; the Prophet answers yes if wickedness becomes widespread. Other reports specify Companions, Badr participants, four named Companions, or two unnamed Qurayshites as addressees; trials are variously identified as civil war, error, unopposed wrong, wealth and children, innovations, or punishment.
rows.anchor: وفي مسلم من حديث زينب بنت جحش سألت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الزبير بن العوام
rows.claim: At the Battle of the Camel, al-Zubayr said he realized only then that the verse concerned the present conflict, not merely its original addressees.
rows.anchor: ما علمت أنا أردنا بهذه الآية إلا اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “it will not strike only the wrongdoers” can modify “trial”; emphatic nūn with a negative is disputed, but the author permits it, citing poetry where emphatic nūn follows la with separation.
rows.anchor: والجملة من قوله لا تصيبن خبرية صفة لقوله فتنة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ parses the clause as an answer to the command, as in “dismount lest it throw you” and the warning to enter homes lest Solomon's army crush you; the author says the analogy fails because the verse does not form the same condition and result.
rows.anchor: وزعم الفراء أن الجملة جواب للأمر نحو قولك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other parses take the clause as a prohibition after the command, as an answer to a deleted oath, or as a negative made affirmative for emphatic nūn; the author rejects al-Zamakhshari's account of al-Farraʾ as compounding the grammatical error.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن قوله لا تصيبن جواب قسم محذوف

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud, ʿAli, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Baqir, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, and Abu al-ʿAliya read “it will surely strike” with lam, warning only wrongdoers; Ibn Masʿud is also reported to read “a trial that strikes.” Al-Naqqash and al-Zubayr give other variants.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد هذا قراءة ابن مسعود وعلي وزيد بن ثابت والباقر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad, al-Farraʾ, and al-Zajjaj explain the canonical form as prohibitive; Ibn Jinni derives it from an extended lam with the resulting alif, while another explanation deletes that alif for ease.
rows.anchor: وخرج المبرد والفراء والزجاج قراءة لا تصيبن على أن تكون ناهية

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash takes “may it not strike” as a supplication; the author infers that he wanted to avoid emphatic nūn after a negative, but the prayer would then exclude no one from the trial.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش لا تصيبن هو على معنى الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parse ends the general warning at “fear a trial,” then begins a prohibition to wrongdoers not to expose themselves to injustice lest the trial strike them specifically; other parses make it a prohibition after a command. The possibilities reduce to prayer, prohibition, command-response, and adjectival constructions.
rows.anchor: وتم الكلام عند قوله واتقوا فتنة وهو خطاب عام للمؤمنين
